:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 7 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$

$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 1 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 7 & 10 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 3 & 6 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 8\end{bmatrix}

	\right].

	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 1 & 1\end{array}

$$

	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 7\end{array}

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?

$$
A=
\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows of $A$ are $-1$, $-4$ and $8$, respectively.

$$
A
=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-1} & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-4} & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{8} & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the answer is $-1+(-4)+8=3.$

A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 8\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$



The first non-zero entry on each row (from left to right) is called the **leading entry** of that row.

- In the matrix $A,$ the leading entries are $a_{11}=2,$ $a_{22}=3,$ $a_{32}=1,$ and $a_{43}=5.$

- In the matrix $B,$ the leading entries are $b_{11}=1,$ $b_{22}=3,$ $b_{33}=-2,$ and $b_{44}=2.$ The $5$th row has no leading entry.

The leading entries are highlighted below.



$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 6 & 9 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 4 & 7 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{5} & 8\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 5 & 2 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 4 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-2} & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0}\end{bmatrix}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following augmented matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The first matrix is not in row echelon form since $a_{32} \neq 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The third matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry $a_{22}$ lies to the left of the leading entry $a_{13}$ (condition II is violated).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 1 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & {\color{black}0} & 1 \\ \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & {\color{red}1} & {\color{red}1} & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 7 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C= \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 1 \\ {\color{red}0} & {\color{red}0} \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B= \begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 7 & 10 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 3 & 6 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 8\end{bmatrix}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the matrix $A$ given below.
Which entries of $A$ could be replaced by $0$ in order to get a matrix in row echelon form?

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 11 & 10 & 9 \\ 0 & 4 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & -1 & 6 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that by replacing $a_{32}$, $a_{42}$, and $a_{43}$ with $0$, we get a matrix in row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned}A  &= \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 11 & 10 & 9 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 7 & 8 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}-1}} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{6} & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}2}} & 4\end{bmatrix} \\ &\longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 11 & 10 & 9 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4} & 7 & 8 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{6} & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{4}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Operations That Would Transform a Matrix To Row Echelon Form

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider our matrices $A$ and $B$ once more, with the leading entries highlighted.



$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 6 & 9 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{{\color{red}1}} & 4 & 7 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{5} & 8\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 5 & 2 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} & 4 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-2} & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0}\end{bmatrix}
$$



We say that a matrix is in **row echelon form** if it satisfies the following conditions:

I. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

II. Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

Here, $B$ is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, $A$ is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row $(a_{32}={\color{red}1})$ is placed just below the leading entry of the second row $(a_{22}=3).$

Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have *stairs* where each step (represented by a leading entry $\bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}$) has a height of $1.$

![](images/67/67f83c454e59d16ae80cf67a19b19f968182251a2e5d1b405e2c422e0313d5b7.png)

Finally, an *augmented* matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?

$$
A=
\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows of $A$ are $-1$, $-4$ and $8$, respectively.

$$
A
=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-1} & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-4} & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{8} & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the answer is $-1+(-4)+8=3.$
